Microscopic vortex braiding from many-body Berry phases
Lu Zhang, Shang-qiang Ning, Hoi Chun Po, Xue-Yang Song, ∗ and Xuzhe Ying †
Department of Physics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Clear Water Bay, Hong Kong, China and
Center for Theoretical Condensed Matter Physics,
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Clear Water Bay, Hong Kong, China
(Dated: October 22, 2026)
Kitaev’s sixteen-fold way relates (2 + 1)D invertible fermionic phases to bosonic topological or-
ders obtained by gauging fermion parity, where the statistics ofπ-vortices are determined by the
Majorana Chern numberν M mod 16. For evenν M, the vortices obey Abelian fusion yet can carry
nontrivial braiding phases that are subtle to access microscopically. We show that these vortex
braiding phases can be extracted as a many-body Berry phase accumulated along a fully gapped
adiabatic cycle that interpolates between the four twisted boundary conditions on a torus. We
demonstrate the computation in free-fermion lattice models with tunableν M. We further provide
an interpretation of vortex braiding phase in terms of fermion-parity fractionalization. Utilizing a
bilayer construction and gauging only the total fermion parity, a toric code topological order en-
riched by a globalZ 2 symmetry is realized. The symmmetry fractionalization data dictates the
fractionalized fermion parity on the vortices.
I. INTRODUCTION
Topological order [1–4] describes gapped quantum
phases that lie beyond the Landau symmetry-breaking
paradigm. Topologically ordered quantum states ex-
hibit universal properties that underpin fault-tolerant
quantum computation[5], including long-range entangle-
ment [6, 7], anyonic excitations with fractional statistics
[4, 8, 9], and robust topological ground-state degeneracy
[2, 10].
Topology and symmetry are intricately correlated. In
the exotic symmetry-enriched topological orders (SET)
[11–15], global symmetry acts nontrivially on the anyons,
for instance by permuting anyon types and/or by endow-
ing them with fractional symmetry charges (a phenom-
ena known as symmetry fractionalization). On the other
hand, a subset of topologically ordered states is closely
related to the invertible states, including symmetry-
protected topological (SPT) phases of matter [16] and
fermionic invertible states [4]. Indeed, Levin-Gu’s work
[16] classifies bosonic SPT by the anyon braiding rule
via gauging the protecting symmetry. The classification
scheme matches the group cohomological classification of
bosonic SPT [17, 18].
Similarly, Kitaev’s seminal work [4] provides a sharp
incarnation of the general idea that (2+1)D fermionic
phases can be mapped to bosonic topological orders
by gauging fermion parity, i.e., by a two-dimensional
bosonization scheme [4, 19–23]. In this correspondence,
a gapped invertible fermion phase with Majorana Chern
numberν M gives rise to a parity-gauged topological or-
der, whose anyon content and statistics depend only on
νM mod 16. For example, a trivial atomic insulator and
s-wave superconductor is mapped to a toric code model;
ap+ipsuperconductor to the Ising topological order.

A central role is played byπ-flux excitations (π-
vortices). For odd Chern number,π-vortices bind an
odd number of Majorana modes, leading to (at least) one
Majorana mode pinned at zero energy. The fusion ofπ-
vortices is sensitive to the microscopic details. Namely,
two Majorana modes hybridize into a complex fermion
which can be filled or empty. Hence, the Hilbert space
of twoπ-vortices is two-dimensional, dictating a non-
abelian fusion rule. The associated non-abelian statistics
was carefully studied and underlies topological quantum
computing [5, 24–28].
For even Majorana Chern number, theπ-vortices fol-
low an abelian fusion rule but nontheless can still carry
nontrivial topological spins and mutual braiding phases,
which is the focus of current work. The representative
systems with even Majorana Chern number include inte-
ger quantum Hall state [29] and Chern insulators [30–32],
withU(1) charge conservation. Due to theU(1) symme-
try, the fusion and braiding statistics ofπ-vortices are
easy to deduce. Relying on the topological stability, the
same properties forπ-vortices are expected to hold in
cases whenU(1) symmetry is explicitly broken toZ f
2
fermion parity. In this work, we aim at understanding
and computing the properties ofπ-vortices in systems
with onlyZ f
2 fermion parity symmetry.
In principle, vortex braiding statistics can be accessed
fromadiabaticallytransporting one vortex around an-
other. This requires the knowledge on either the string
operators for the vortices [33, 34] or a set of Hamiltonians
or states that form an adiabatic path. In practice, how-
ever, string operators can be rather complicated except a
few fixed-point cases; on the other hand, when explicitly
moving a vortex in a microscopic lattice model, energy
levels of the vortex states can cross (note that we do not
mean bulk gap closing), which poisons the adiabaticity.
Before proceeding, we should mention that there have
been various proposal in computing topological data from
microscopic states [35–39].
In this work, we provide an explicit microscopic cal-

For demonstration, the calculation is done with the aid
of a free-fermion model with tunable Chern number on
torus with onlyZ f
2 fermion parity symmetry. We consider
an adiabatic evolution connecting four possible twisted
boundary conditions on a torus and compute the many-
body Berry phase. It turns out that the computed
many-body Berry phase matches with the vortex braid-
ing phase. We further show that the vortex braiding
phase can be interpreted as fermion-parity fractionaliza-
tion. This is suggesting that atν M = 2 theπ-vortices
carry “half” fermion parity, analogous to the halfU(1)
charge of theπ-vortices in integer quantum Hall states.
This notion of half or fractionalized fermion parity is
most transparent when we consider a bilayer fermionic
system and its bosonization. The data for symmetry
enrichment (or more specifically the defect fusion rule)
dictates the symmetry fractionalization.
The remainder of the manuscript is organized as fol-
lows. Section II discusses our computation of vortex
braiding phase. Section III constructs certain symme-
try enriched topological order from a bilayer system. The
symmetry enriched data dictates fermion parity fraction-
alization. Sec. IV concludes this manuscript with fur-
ther discussions. App. A introduces the fermion model
and App. B outlines the computation of overlap between
Gaussian states.
II. VOR TEX BRAIDING PHASE FROM
ADIABA TIC EVOLUTION
In this section, we provide an explicit microscopic
calculation of vortex braiding phase. As schematically
shown in Fig. 1, the key idea is to mimic the global loop
operators of the parity-gauged topologically ordered state
on a torus by a sequence of adiabatic deformations on the
corresponding invertible fermion state. This adiabatic
path smoothly connects four possible (twisted) boundary
conditions for the fermionic model. We then compute the
many-body Berry phase along this closed adiabatic cycle
and identify it with the vortex braiding phase.
On a torus, a topological order exhibits a topologically
protected ground-state degeneracy. From a quantum-
information perspective, the ground-state subspace forms
a code space, and logical operations are implemented by
nonlocal loop operators ˆWa(C) which winds the anyona
along the non-contractible loopC(Fig. 1). For Abelian
anyonsaandb, their mutual braiding phaseθ ab is en-
coded in the commutator of loop operators along the two
non-contractible loopsC 1 andC 2:
eiθab = ˆWa(C1) ˆWb(C2) ˆW −1
a (C1) ˆW −1
b (C2).(1)
In what follows we focus on systems with even Majorana
Chern numbersν M = 0 and 2. In Kitaev’s sixteen-fold
way, the topological order is obtained by gauging fermion
parity or bosonization. For nonzero Chern number, it
is difficult to write down the microscopic loop operators
explicitly, and thus Eq. (1) is not straightforward to eval-
uate directly.
To perform our calculation, we note that states with
twisted boundary conditions in the fermionic theory
can be mapped to the various ground states in the
gauged/bosonized theory. This follows from a useful ob-
servation of the generic 2D bosonization scheme [4, 19–
23]. That is, for a staticZ 2 gauge field configuration, the
Hilbert space of the gauged theory factorizes as
|fermions in the even-parity sector⟩⊗|Z 2 static gauge fields⟩,
(2)
where the fermionic sector may containπvortices deter-
mined by theZ 2 gauge field. The gauged theory sat-
isfies a set of local constraints ˆCi. For instance in the
Verstraete-Cirac mapping [20], the local constraints act
only on the gauge field sector and take the following form:
ˆCi|Z2 static gauge fields⟩=|Z 2 static gauge fields⟩,(3)
State satisfying the all the local constraints correspond to
fermionic system without any fluxes. Violations of these
constraints correspond to local presence ofπ-vortices,
i.e., the flux anyons of the gauged theory.
Note, however, that fluxes can only be created in
pairs in the bosonized theory. Pairs of vortices are con-
nected by a string operator. When a fermion traverses
the string, the fermion state picks up a minus sign.
Hence, winding a vortex around a non-contractible loop
in the bosonized theory leaves behind a string, which im-
plements a twisted boundary condition experienced by
fermions just as flux insertion into the torus would result
in.
Motivated by this observation, we identify the four
groundstates in Fig. 1 with four twisted boundary condi-
tions for the fermionic theory on a torus. We then expect
that the Berry phase accumulated along the gapped adi-
abatic path connecting these ground states under twisted

III. BILA YER ST ACKING:Z 2 ENRICHED
TORIC CODE AND FERMION P ARITY

In this section, we sharpen the notion of fractional
fermion parity by considering a bilayer system and the
relatedZ 2-enriched topological order. A well-studied ex-
ample is stacking two layers with Majorana Chern num-
berν M =±1, which realizes a toric code with a global
Z2 symmetry exchangingeandmanyons [11, 13, 14].
In this section, we study a bilayer system withν M =±2
and show that this realizes a toric code state withZ 2
symmetry fractionalization.
To be more concrete, we consider a bilayer fermionic
system with global symmetryZ f,t

C. Deduce symmetry fractionalization from defect
fusion rule
Comparing Eq. (9) and Eq. (12), the defect fusion rule
is indeed changed. Mathematically, the difference in the
defect fusion rule is classified by the second group coho-
mologyH 2(Z2,C e =Z 2 ×Z 2). (Note that in both cases
above, the deconfined anyons inC e can be identified with
those of toric code.) This classification of defect fusion
rule is mathematically the same as that for symmetry
fractionalization [11].
Pictorially, the changed in the symmetry fractionaliza-
tion from defect fusion rule can be read off from diagrams
in Fig. 4 and see Ref. [11, 41] for more detailed discus-
sions. In Fig. 4, we start from the defect fusion rule for
the bilayer with zero Chern numbers in step (1) and then
go through step (2) and (3) to implement the change in
defect fusion rule and derive the corresponding change in
the symmetry fractionalization pattern.
In step (1), we pick the reference symmetry defect
1g ∈ C g. An anyonx e ∈ C e is transported across the
branch-cut of two symmetry defects 1g’s. (Two reference
symmetry defects fuse into the vacuum sector 1∈ C e.)
This process is equivalent to applyingZ 2 symmetry ac-
tiontwiceon the anyon statex e. In comparison, we could
apply the identity operation on the anyon state as in step
(2). The difference in how symmetry action is applied as
in steps (1) and (2) is dictated by aU(1) phaseη x(g,g).
Indeed, in cases where the anyonx e carries fractional
symmetry charges, applyingZ 2 symmetry action twice
is not the same as identity operation, resulting in the
nontrivial phaseη x(g,g).
From step (2) to step (3), the defect fusion rule is
effectively changed. In step (2), there is no harm to
add anabeliananyon loop (blue) in a distant regime.
This abelian anyon is labeled asω(g,g), which is a
mapping from two group elements to abelian anyons:
ω:Z 2 ×Z 2 → C e. In step (3), we expand this anyon
loop, bring it close to the fusion junction and let the
anyonx e cross the anyon loop. In this way, the defect
fusion rule is effectively changed to 1 g ×1 g =ω(g,g)×1.
The diagrams in steps (2) and (3) are related by the
U(1) braiding phase [M xe,ω(g,g)]∗ between anyonsx e and
ω(g,g).
Effectively from step (1) to step (3), the symmetry
action follows a different associative rule, dictated by the
newU(1) phaseη ′
x(g,g) =η x(g,g)[M xe,ω(g,g)]∗.
For the bilayer system under consideration, presum-
ably the case with two layers of vanishing Chern num-
ber is trivial in symmetry fractionalization, namely
ηx(g,g) = 1. Following the discussion of defect fu-
sion rule, we can identifyω(g,g) =ϵ t, see Eq. (9)
and Eq. (12). For the vortices, the braiding phase
[Mxe,ω(g,g)]∗ =−1 forx e ∈ {e, m} ⊂ C e. Hence, after
changing the defect fusion rule, the applyingZ 2 symme-
try twice differs from identity transformation by a minus
sign. This is indicating that the vortices carry fractional
Z2 charge, i.e., nontrivial symmetry fractionalization pat-

teger symmetry charge, which is reflected in theU(1)
phases [Mxe,ω(g,g)]∗ = 1 forx e ∈ {1, ϵ} ⊂ C e.
IV. CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION
In conclusion, we have provided a microscopic route to
the abelian braiding statistics ofπ-vortices in (2 + 1)D
fermionic invertible phases with even Majorana Chern
number. By constructing a fully gapped adiabatic cycle
that interpolates among the four twisted boundary con-
ditions on a torus, we showed that the vortex braiding
phase can be extracted as a quantized many-body Berry
phase. In free-fermion lattice models with tunableν M,
the Berry phase reproduces the expected values (e.g., 0
forν M = 0 andπ/2 forν M = 2).
We further connected the braiding phase to symmetry-
enrichment data via a bilayer construction. Upon gaug-
ing only the total fermion parity, the resultingZ 2-
enriched toric-code order exhibits a nontrivial defect fu-
sion rule that encodes a fractionalZ2 symmetry action on
eandmanyons (as boundstates of vortices from both lay-
ers). In this language, theπ/2 vortex braiding phase sig-
nals a “half” fermion-parity quantum number carried by
the vortex defect, made precise through the induced sym-
metry fractionalization pattern on the deconfined anyons.
Several directions remain open. It would be interesting
to identify a more local diagnostic of fractional fermion
parity that does not rely on torus boundary twists, and
to extend the Berry-phase approach beyond free fermions
to interacting settings [42]. More broadly, we expect our
computation is generalizable to a generic symmetry pro-
tected topological states. The input data include the
symmetry representation on local Hilbert space and an
adiabatic path connecting various flux configurations.
